concept.tagline: Carving mmap/brk regions into thread-local size classes (jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc) for 15–30 ns lock-free malloc/free.

spark.summary: User-space memory allocators like jemalloc, tcmalloc, and mimalloc sit between your application and the OS kernel, carving large mmap/brk regions into thread-local size classes so malloc() and free() complete in ~15–30 ns without global lock contention or virtual memory fragmentation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Default glibc ptmalloc2 optimizes for low metadata overhead, whereas jemalloc, tcmalloc, and mimalloc trade small per-thread caches for dramatic reductions in multi-core lock contention and long-running RSS fragmentation.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A **user-space allocator** (`ptmalloc2`, `jemalloc`, `tcmalloc`, `mimalloc`) batches coarse OS `mmap`/`brk` syscalls into **segregated size classes** (8 B, 16 B, 32 B, ..., 32 KB) to bound internal fragmentation under ~12.5%.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Thread-Local Cache -> Size-Class Arena -> OS Kernel mmap (malloc(64B) -> Thread / CPU Cache -> Size-Class Arena -> Kernel mmap/madvise); jemalloc Span Lifecycle (Active -> Dirty -> MADV_DONTNEED) (ACTIVE SPAN -> DIRTY CACHE -> UNBACKED).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare allocators on thread-cache RSS, decay speed, and profiling. In Kubernetes, set `dirty_decay_ms: 1000–2000` so freed spans return to the kernel before the cgroup OOM killer fires, while avoiding `dirty_decay_ms: 0` (which burns 5–12% extra.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore container OOM killer behavior, CoW memory bloat, and cache-line false sharing.

learningJourney.title: What is a User-Space Memory Allocator
learningJourney.explanation:
A **user-space allocator** (`ptmalloc2`, `jemalloc`, `tcmalloc`, `mimalloc`) batches coarse OS `mmap`/`brk` syscalls into **segregated size classes** (8 B, 16 B, 32 B, ..., 32 KB) to bound internal fragmentation under ~12.5%.

**Thread-local caches (`tcache`)** or **per-CPU caches** (via Linux `rseq` in tcmalloc) serve 95%+ of allocations lock-free in 10–25 ns without hitting arena mutexes.

sectionDiagram.title: Thread-Local Cache -> Size-Class Arena -> OS Kernel mmap

cards.label: 1. Segregated Bins
cards.detail: Fixed size classes eliminate free-list linear scans and bound internal waste.

cards.label: 2. Thread-Local Hit
cards.detail: 95%+ of small allocations pop from tcache with zero cross-core synchronization.

cards.label: 3. Page Return
cards.detail: Dirty decay timers return freed spans to the OS via madvise(MADV_DONTNEED).

sectionDiagram.summary: Layered thread caches + segregated arenas keep small allocations fast while returning unused pages to the kernel.

learningJourney.title: Why ptmalloc2 arenas and remote-frees blow up container RSS
learningJourney.explanation:
Every `malloc`, `Vec::push`, or RocksDB/Netty off-heap buffer hits the allocator. Two production pathologies strike containerized services:
- **ptmalloc2 Arena Proliferation**: glibc spawns 64 MB arenas up to `8 * host_CPU_count`. A 4 GB cgroup container on a 64-core host can explode virtual/resident memory.
- **Producer-Consumer Remote-Free Skew**: I/O threads allocate buffers and worker threads free them, starving the producer's `tcache` and forcing slow arena locks.

ideas.title: Cap Arenas in Containers
ideas.description: Set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4` for glibc or configure `jemalloc` `narenas` to `2 * cgroup_cpus`.

ideas.title: mimalloc for Cross-Thread Frees
ideas.description: `mimalloc` shards free lists per page with lock-free atomic remote-free lists, avoiding producer-consumer skew.

learningJourney.title: Tuning jemalloc Dirty Decay & Arenas via MALLOC_CONF
learningJourney.explanation: Balance RSS tightness (`dirty_decay_ms`) against kernel page-fault CPU (`MADV_DONTNEED` re-zeroing).
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```bash
# Production jemalloc tuning for a 4-vCPU container running RocksDB / Rust / C++
export LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2
export MALLOC_CONF="narenas:8,dirty_decay_ms:2000,muzzy_decay_ms:5000,tcache:true,prof:true,prof_prefix:/tmp/jeprof"

# Fallback if staying on glibc ptmalloc2 in high-core Kubernetes hosts:
export MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: ptmalloc2 vs. jemalloc vs. tcmalloc vs. mimalloc
learningJourney.explanation: Compare allocators on thread-cache RSS, decay speed, and profiling.

benefits: Low long-running fragmentation, built-in heap profiling (`prof:true`), predictable `dirty_decay_ms`.
costs: Slightly larger metadata footprint than ptmalloc2.

benefits: Ultra-low latency with per-CPU caches instead of per-thread caches (saves RAM at 500+ threads).
costs: Tighter coupling to modern Linux kernels (`rseq`).

benefits: Compact, fast, and excels at cross-thread producer-consumer deallocation.
costs: Less mature built-in production heap-sampling tooling than jemalloc.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can default glibc ptmalloc2 cause unexpected RSS growth in a 4 GB Kubernetes container running on a 64-core host?

options.text: ptmalloc2 disables virtual memory paging inside containers
options.feedback: Paging is controlled by the kernel cgroup, not ptmalloc2.

options.text: ptmalloc2 scales its 64 MB arena limit up to 8 * host_CPU_count, ignoring cgroup CPU quotas unless MALLOC_ARENA_MAX is set
options.feedback: Correct: on a 64-core host, glibc can create hundreds of arenas; cap MALLOC_ARENA_MAX or use jemalloc with cgroup-sized narenas.

options.text: ptmalloc2 never frees memory back to the heap
options.feedback: ptmalloc2 frees blocks into arenas, but arena fragmentation across many arenas inflates RSS.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
